summary: Describes Real-time Inter-network Defense (RID), a system for network providers and security incident response teams to communicate and trace security incidents such as worms, phishing, and denial of service across networks. It is informational. It was replaced by RFC 6545.

plainLanguage.summary: When a computer attack spreads across many networks, the people protecting them need to talk to each other. RID is a way to do that. It was replaced by RFC 6545.

questions: how do networks share security incident information
what are the rid message types
how does rid trace spoofed attacks
subtitle: A messaging system that lets network providers trace attacks upstream and ask each other to stop them, in near real time.

tldr.problem: Tracing an attack with a spoofed source address across several networks has no established way to continue the trace, so an administrator may just phone the next network and ask.
tldr.mechanism: RID wraps IODEF incident reports in an XML envelope with six message types, including TraceRequest and Investigation. Each provider decides whether to continue, and signed and optionally encrypted messages carry policy, packet samples and the path so far.
tldr.outcome: The document says RID has found use within international research communities but has not been widely adopted in other sectors. It is Informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 6545.

today: RFC 6045 is an Informational document that has been obsoleted by RFC 6545. Its own text says RID has found use within international research communities but has not been widely adopted in other sectors. The matching transport specification, RFC 6046, was likewise replaced by RFC 6546.

sections.title: The Problem of Cross-Network Tracing
sections.content:
Incident handling covers detection, reporting, identification and mitigation of attacks such as system compromises, phishing and denial of service (DoS). Tracing is hardest when the source address is spoofed, logs are deleted, or the sources are too many. Network providers (NPs) already have tools to trace traffic inside their own backbone, but when traffic crosses several networks, the RFC says there is no established mechanism for continuing the trace. An administrator might place a phone call to the next upstream network.

Real-time Inter-network Defense (RID) is the communication mechanism proposed to fill that gap. It carries incident data as XML using the Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF, RFC 5070) plus a RID extension. It is designed to work with a variety of existing and future detection, tracing and response approaches, and to let each provider decide whether a trace should continue.

The abstract states that RID has found use within the international research communities but has not been widely adopted in other sectors, and that the document is published for those communities and for others considering such solutions.
sections.plainLanguage: When an attack passes through many networks, each network only sees its own piece. RID lets them hand the investigation from one to the next instead of making phone calls.

sections.title: Spoofed Sources, Traces and Packet Samples
sections.content:
The type of message used depends on whether the source address is believed valid. If it is spoofed, a detailed packet trace (TraceRequest) is needed to find the real source, moving upstream network by network. If the address is valid, routing information can show which provider is closest to the source, and an Investigation request asks that provider to help.

To trace a packet, an example packet from the attack travels with the request. Based on research on hash-based IP traceback, RID requires the first 28 invariant bytes of an IPv4 packet, which is the masked IP header plus the first 8 bytes of payload, and the first 48 invariant bytes of an IPv6 packet. Limiting the sample this way avoids sharing sensitive data from the rest of the payload. The full packet may be included as well, and is stored in the IODEF RecordItem class.

Distributed attacks may need many TraceRequests, and attacks using zombies may need one trace to find the zombies and another to find the controlling server. The RFC lists several things that make tracing hard, such as multiple sources, a very small number of packets from each source, and traffic to valid essential services.
sections.plainLanguage: To find where a bad letter came from, you send the next post office a photocopy of the front of the envelope. RID says exactly how much of the copy is needed, and no more.

sections.title: Providers, Consortiums and Topology
sections.content:
Each network provider runs an incident handling system (IHS) that sends and receives RID messages and can connect to its network management system, intrusion detection and trace tools. Smaller providers might use a neutral third party for this role. A consortium is a group of providers or response teams that agree to use RID under shared policy and a secure transport, which is defined separately in RFC 6046.

The basic topology is a direct connection between two RID systems at a network border. Within a consortium, peers may follow routing peers for an iterative trace, or form a mesh when the source address is known and a more direct path to the provider nearest the source is useful. Broadcasting a request to a full mesh is possible but not advisable, because many networks would spend resources on an unnecessary trace.

The RFC recommends that each provider dedicate a 24x7 hotline for incident communication and that the RID network be out of band or protected. RID requests must be legitimate security incidents and not used for purposes such as sabotage or censorship. Each RID system should be configurable to ask for operator approval or to continue traces automatically, and a system that sees its own information in the path of a TraceRequest must stop the trace and alert staff about the loop.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks that trust each other join a club with shared rules. Club members can pass investigation requests along, but only for real emergencies, and each can say no.

sections.title: The Six Messages and the RID Schema
sections.content:
RID defines six message types, all based on IODEF. A TraceRequest starts or continues an upstream trace. A RequestAuthorization goes back to the requester to say whether the current network approved the trace. A Result tells the originator that the source was located, or reports the actions taken for an Investigation. An Investigation request is used when the source is believed not spoofed. A Report files an incident with no action requested, and an IncidentQuery asks a trusted RID system about an incident, with a Report as the reply.

RID adds three classes in the iodef-rid namespace, which acts as an envelope around the IODEF document. RIDPolicy carries the message type, the destination, the incident ID, policy region and traffic type, and can be read without decrypting the incident data. RequestStatus reports whether a trace was Approved, Denied or Pending, with an optional justification such as SystemResource or Authentication. IncidentSource reports whether a source was found and lists the nodes.

The MsgDestination value is RIDSystem when the address names the next RID system, or SourceOfIncident when it is the address of the incident source, which is used to route an Investigation request. The namespace is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:iodef-rid-1.0.
sections.plainLanguage: There are six kinds of notes: please trace this, yes I will or no I will not, found it, please check this, just so you know, and have you seen this. Each note has a label on the outside so mail handlers know where it goes without opening it.

sections.title: How a Trace Proceeds
sections.content:
In an upstream trace, the network that detects the attack sends a TraceRequest to the next upstream provider. That provider answers with a RequestAuthorization, then locates the traffic and repeats the process with its own upstream neighbor. When a provider finds the source on its own network, it sends a Result to the originator, using the path information carried in the request. A Result is encrypted for the originator, and if the originator cannot decrypt or authenticate it, it sends back a RequestAuthorization.

A Pending status is generated automatically after a 2-minute timeout when nobody has approved or declined the trace. If a request is Denied, both the originator and the sending peer must receive the message, so that the sending peer can try to stop or mitigate the traffic as close to the source as possible. Multiple traces of one incident share an IncidentID, with a separate instance number when a trace diverges.

An IncidentQuery reply may contain several incidents. The recommended limit is 5 per report, to keep documents from becoming too large.
sections.plainLanguage: Each post office says 'yes, I will look' and passes the request on. When one finally finds the sender, it reports straight back to whoever started the search.

sections.title: Security, Trust and Privacy
sections.content:
Communication between providers' RID systems must be protected. Authenticated encrypted tunnels MUST be used, and trust relationships are based on consortiums and public key infrastructure (PKI) cross-certification. The originator of a TraceRequest or Investigation request MUST use a detached signature on at least one of the original IP packets, so upstream participants can authenticate the origin. For all message types, the full IODEF/RID document MUST be signed with an enveloped signature by the sending peer. Documents may also be encrypted with XML Encryption, while RIDPolicy stays in clear text so intermediate parties can route messages.

Receivers MUST be able to verify that a sender is valid and trusted, using digital signatures with X.509 version 3 certificates, and pre-shared keys, if used, must follow RFC 4279. Privacy is a major concern: customers MUST understand that their data can and will be sent to other providers to complete a trace, unless a service level agreement says otherwise. Consortiums are expected to set guidelines that include protecting RID systems and a PKI.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages are signed like a letter with a unique wax seal and can be locked in a box. Everyone has to know up front that their information may be shared to finish an investigation.

messages.label: TraceRequest
messages.note: NP-1 detects the attack and asks the upstream NP to trace.

messages.label: TraceRequest
messages.note: NP-2 locates the origin through its upstream NP.

messages.label: Result
messages.note: NP-3 locates the attack source on its network.

items.label: TraceRequest
items.desc: Start or continue an upstream trace.

items.label: RequestAuthorization
items.desc: Tell the requester if the trace is approved, denied or pending.

items.label: Investigation
items.desc: Ask the provider nearest a valid source to act.

items.label: Report
items.desc: File an incident with no action requested.

items.label: IncidentQuery
items.desc: Ask a trusted system about an incident.
